latin: Corpus Christi ex se fuit impassibile.
translation: The body of Christ was, of itself, incapable of suffering.
translation_note: 'Impassibile': incapable of suffering or undergoing change, a technical term in the theology of Christ's body and of the resurrection.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch6, from Latin at farmer1998:12255

sources.text: John Duns Scotus, Ordinatio 4, d. 49, pars 2, q. unica ('Utrum corpus hominis beati post resurrectionem erit impassibile'; Opera omnia, vol. 14, Vatican City, 2013, pp. 395–411)
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit identifies this question, on whether the risen body will be incapable of suffering, as the discussion behind thesis 12

doctrine: The thesis concerns the impassibility of Christ's body considered in itself, apart from the Passion. Farmer directs the reader to thesis 2.15, on the impassibility of glorified bodies after the resurrection ('Impassibilitas corporum post resurrectionem erit ex pleno dominio animae super corpus', farmer1998:11433), and to its accompanying note (farmer1998:12341). Edelheit states that thesis 12 holds the body of Christ to have been in itself incapable of suffering, and identifies the discussion in Scotus's Ordinatio, book 4, distinction 49, part 2, question unica, titled 'whether the body of the blessed person after resurrection will be incapable of suffering' (edelheit2022:14473).
historiography: Edelheit's identification of the Ordinatio question, and his naming of its formal title, are the only treatment of thesis 12 among the sources consulted (edelheit2022:14473).

quotations.text: Thesis 12 states that the body of Christ was in itself incapable of suffering

not_established: Whether Pico draws on Scotus's arguments for the resurrected body's impassibility specifically, or shares only the conclusion, is not stated by Edelheit in the material consulted.
